newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Cohen says Chinese arms sales to Iran can backfire.
newsitem.headline: Cohen says Chinese arms sales to Iran can backfire.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Wednesday warned China that its sale of anti-ship cruise missiles to Iran could one day backfire in a new Gulf conflict, halting the flow of oil to Beijing and the world.

''In the long run, it contradicts China's self interests. China has become a net importer of energy. They depend upon having access to energy coming out of the Gulf,'' Cohen said on his way home after a visit to Saudi Arabia and other states in the volatile region.

He spoke to reporters aboard his jet a day after revealing that Iran this month successfully tested a new air launched anti-ship cruise missile obtained from China. He warned Tehran against trying to close the Gulf which supplies half of the world's oil.

''To the extent that their (Chinese) arms sales, which provide them with immediate capital, increase the instability in the region, they could very well find that their access would be cut off in a future time,'' Cohen said.
''So it is a short-term type of game that they might acquire by selling the weapons. Over the long term, it only helps to destabilise the region and go against their own self interest.''

The United States has repeatedly pressed China and Russia not to sell weapons to Iran, which Washington accuses of supporting terrorism and developing ambitions to control the narrow mouth of the Gulf.
Iran has spent billions of dollars on weapons in recent years, including three Russian diesel-powered submarines and Russian warplanes in addition to Chinese missiles and patrol boats.
Cohen visited Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, and Oman on a five day trip which ended on Wednesday in Oman's capital Muscat.
Some Gulf officials have pressed Washington to talk to Iran rather than pushing to isolate it.
But Cohen said the members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) were generally unanimous in their support of the U.S. effort to contain Iraq and Iran in the region.

''What I expressed to every leader that I met was the United States' commitment to the region, our strength and reliability and the fact that we are dedicated to continue our relationship and build up on it,'' Cohen said.

''On one issue they were unanimous and that is that they supported the United States' policies. They support what we are doing. They intend to continue in a cooperative relationship with us so that we can preserve stability and peace in the region.''
